name: Cardiff Castle
label: Cardiff Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Castle Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Castle Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1093259587: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cardiff Castle' (332 m across).
notes: Roman fort, Norman keep and Victorian Gothic Revival apartments.

text.description:
Cardiff Castle sits right in the city centre, and it is really two buildings in one: a medieval Norman castle and a Victorian Gothic mansion. The Normans built the first castle in the late 11th century on top of a 3rd-century Roman fort. Much later, the 3rd Marquess of Bute paid for William Burges to remodel it in Gothic revival style. After the Roman remains were found, Roman-style walls and a gatehouse were built into the design. That mix of eras is why the outside photographs so well: stone walls, towers and a grand entrance front all packed into one view.

The easiest free shot is from the pavement on Castle Street, looking up the street towards the entrance gate. The street acts as a natural frame and leads the eye straight to the gatehouse. If you have time, Bute Park is another place to photograph the castle from, with the castle walls and towers rising above the trees and paths.

A fact worth knowing as you look at the walls: during the Second World War, large air raid shelters were built inside them, big enough for up to 1,800 people. The castle was given to the City of Cardiff in 1947 and is now a visitor attraction and events venue. Keep your phone ready for people walking through the frame, and take a few shots so you can pick the one with the clearest view of the gate.
text.geographic_location: Cardiff Castle is in the city centre of Cardiff, and Castle Street is the street where you take this shot. Bute Park is another place to photograph the castle from.
text.directions_text: Head for the city centre of Cardiff and then to Castle Street. From there it is only a couple of minutes on foot to the castle itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the street, the gate and some sky in one frame. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or traffic leave you too little room, and keep the castle in the middle so the edges are not stretched. Try 2x for a tighter shot of the gatehouse.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Castle Street (view towards the castle entrance gate). The castle's gatehouse and entrance front, framed by the street leading up to it. On the pavement, and face north towards the castle entrance gate. From here the photo shows the gatehouse and entrance front framed by the street leading up to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the street so it leads towards the gate. Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. Wait for a gap in the people on the pavement. For something different, Bute Park shows the walls and towers above the trees, with paths in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gatehouse to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the stonework. If the street is busy, take a short burst or a Live Photo and choose the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day and adjust your exposure to suit it.

text.access_note: Castle Street is a public pavement with no ticket needed, but the castle interior is ticketed, so check the official site before you go for grounds access and any closures.
claims_not_in_sources: Castle Street is a public pavement and the view from it needs no ticket (from the researched viewpoint notes).

name: Principality Stadium
label: Principality Stadium
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1287329038: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Principality Stadium' (331 m across).
notes: Wales' national stadium in the city centre, home of Welsh rugby.

text.description:
The Principality Stadium is the national stadium of Wales. It was known as the Millennium Stadium until early 2016, when it was renamed under a sponsorship deal. It opened in June 1999, built for that year's Rugby World Cup, on the Cardiff Arms Park site where the old National Stadium stood. The new stadium was turned to run north to south rather than west to east. It holds 73,931 people, which makes it the largest stadium in Wales. It also has a fully retractable roof, and it has hosted football finals, concerts and even motorsport as well as rugby.

It photographs well because of its sheer size. The curved steel stands and roof structure make strong shapes, and the stadium sits right among the city streets, so you can place people or street life against it for scale. Up close the building is too big to fit into one frame at the default lens (1x), so think in sections: a sweep of wall, the roof line, a gate with people walking past. Turn on the gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight, and step back as far as the pavement allows before you shoot. On match and event days the surroundings are busy and some areas may be closed off, so allow extra time and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in Cardiff, beside the River Taff, with the River Walk on its western side. It stands next to Park Street, Wood Street and Westgate Street. Cardiff Arms Park, the home of Cardiff RFC, is next door to the north.
text.directions_text: Start from Cardiff: the stadium is next to Park Street, Wood Street and Westgate Street, with the River Walk by the River Taff on its western side. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x). You are very close to the stadium, so the ultra-wide is the lens that lets you fit in a good part of its walls and roof. Keep the default lens (1x) for tighter shots of details such as gates, signs and the structure.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Face north-east so the middle of the building fills the view ahead. Hold the phone level and angle it up slightly to take in the roof line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the stadium's vertical edges up with them so the walls don't lean inwards. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for one big shot, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a detail shot. Include a few passers-by to show the scale. If you want a longer view of the whole stadium, the River Taff side to the west gives more room to step back.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stadium wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. Keep the phone level, because tilting it up makes the sides slope inwards. If you use the ultra-wide, keep people out of the extreme edges of the frame, where they look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a day with some cloud or soft light, and go outside event days if you want a calm view. Early morning is usually the quietest time. On match or concert days the area is much busier, which can add atmosphere but makes it harder to find space.

text.access_note: The area around the stadium is public, but it is a working venue with ticketed events, so check the official site before you go for event days and any restrictions.

name: Wales Millennium Centre
label: Wales Millennium Centr
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/987017194: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wales Millennium Centre' (106 m across).
notes: Arts centre in Cardiff Bay with a bronze-clad facade and giant lettering.

text.description: Wales Millennium Centre is Wales's national arts centre, in the Cardiff Bay area of Cardiff. It photographs well because the building is built from materials that look good up close. The outside is clad in slate in several colours, from purple and blue to green, grey and black. Narrow windows are set between the layers, so the wall looks like rock strata in a sea cliff. Over the Donald Gordon Theatre sits a bronze-coloured dome clad in stainless steel. About 1,350 tonnes of Welsh slate went into the building, and the first phase opened in November 2004. The theatre has 1,896 seats and the whole site covers about 3 hectares, so the building is large. Expect to choose between a wide view of the whole frontage and tighter shots of the textures. For the wide view, step back a little and let the dome and slate fill the frame. For detail, go in on the layers of slate and the narrow windows, where the different colours show best. If someone is walking past, a small figure gives a good sense of scale. Check the official site before you go if you want to photograph inside.
text.geographic_location: The centre is in the Cardiff Bay area of Cardiff. It is the city's main venue for large-scale opera, ballet and musicals.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Cardiff Bay area and look for Wales Millennium Centre. Walk towards the north-east and the dome and slate walls will be in front of you. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the frontage. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are too close to fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the slate layers, the narrow windows and the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You are close, so face north-east and take in the slate walls and the dome. Move a few steps back or sideways to fit more in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the horizontal bands of slate so the building does not lean. Keep the dome in the upper part of the frame and let the layered wall fill the rest. For a second shot, go in close with the telephoto and fill the frame with the colours of the slate and the thin windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the slate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bronze dome and the sky do not wash out. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone still against something solid, or lean on a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the morning or late afternoon brings out the colours of the slate and the glow of the dome. Dusk is also worth trying, but check the weather first, as the slate looks dull on grey days.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the surrounding open space, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules about photographing inside.

name: Senedd
label: Senedd
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Roald Dahl Plass' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Roald Dahl Plass' (relation/11005399): middle (123 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/792763506: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Senedd Estate' (298 m across).
notes: Glass and slate home of the Welsh Parliament on the bay.

text.description:
The Senedd is the home of the Welsh Parliament, the devolved body that scrutinises the Welsh Government and makes laws for Wales on devolved matters such as health, education and transport. For photographers it is the low, modern building with a glass-and-timber frontage, sitting on the waterfront beside the red-brick Pierhead Building. The two buildings make a good contrast of old and new, and the bay water close by adds a clean backdrop.

The body was created in 1999 and was called the National Assembly for Wales until May 2020, when it took the name Senedd Cymru, or Welsh Parliament. You will see both Welsh and English on signs, as both are official languages of its business.

The best all-round view is from Roald Dahl Plass, the open plaza in front of the Senedd. The plaza is free and open to the public. If you want a wider scene, the Cardiff Bay Barrage gives a longer view across the water, taking in the Pierhead Building, the Norwegian Church and Penarth Marina. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the long horizontal lines of the frontage straight, and take a few frames as people move through the plaza. The exterior is the main subject here, so don't plan your visit around going inside.
text.geographic_location: The Senedd stands on the Cardiff Bay waterfront, next to the Pierhead Building and facing the open plaza of Roald Dahl Plass.
text.directions_text: No railway station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check local transport options for getting to the Cardiff Bay waterfront. Once you are in the bay area, walk to Roald Dahl Plass, the open plaza in front of the Senedd. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage with the Pierhead Building beside it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the plaza is busy and you want to keep both buildings and some sky in the frame. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the timber and glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass (open plaza on the waterfront in front of the Senedd, next to the Pierhead Building). The Senedd's glass-and-timber frontage across the open plaza, with the red-brick Pierhead Building alongside and the bay water nearby. From here you see the Senedd's glass-and-timber frontage across the open plaza, with the red-brick Pierhead Building alongside and the bay water nearby. For a wider alternative, walk to the Cardiff Bay Barrage and pick a spot with a clear sightline to the Senedd.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the horizontal edge of the Senedd roof up with a grid line so the building does not look tilted. Leave open plaza in the foreground to give a sense of space, and place the Pierhead Building on one side to balance the modern frontage. From the Barrage, use the water as a foreground and include the Norwegian Church and Penarth Marina for a wider scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Senedd to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright so the glass and timber keep their detail. At dusk or after dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and dusk are suggested for the bay views, and evening shots of the Senedd and Pierhead are common, but there is no single best time. Try one early or late visit if you can.

text.access_note: The plaza outside is free and open to the public, but access to the inside of the Senedd may be limited, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Museum Cardiff
label: National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gorsedd Gardens' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gorsedd Gardens' (way/26569588): middle (175 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11230494: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum Cardiff' (188 m across).
notes: Neoclassical museum of art and natural history in Cathays Park.

text.description: National Museum Cardiff is a large, pale stone building in Cathays Park, the civic centre of the city. It is easiest to photograph from the lawns in front, where the columned portico and wide steps sit in the middle of the frame. The museum was founded in 1905 and received its royal charter in 1907. Building work began in 1912, but the First World War delayed things. It opened to the public in 1922, with the official opening in 1927. The architects were Arnold Dunbar Smith and Cecil Brewer, and the sculpture scheme was devised by Sir W. Goscombe John. Look up around the base of the dome for the lions, which make a good close-up detail. From the gardens the building looks symmetrical and calm, and the grass in the foreground gives your photo a clear sense of depth. The simplest picture is the whole facade with the portico, steps and a strip of lawn. If you want something different, walk up to the steps and shoot between the stone pillars, or step back into the wider park for the museum among the neighbouring civic buildings. People often pass through the gardens, so wait a moment for a clear gap, or use them for scale. Entry has been free in the past, but the museum announced a temporary closure in February 2025, so check the official site for opening times before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Cathays Park, Cardiff's civic centre, among other large public buildings. Gorsedd Gardens, the open lawns where you take the photo, lie directly in front of its entrance.
text.directions_text: There are no station or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for Cathays Park, the civic centre area of Cardiff, from the city centre on foot or by taxi. Ask for the National Museum or Gorsedd Gardens. Once there, stand on the lawns in front of the museum's main entrance, with the building to the north-west of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the building will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, the sculptures and the lions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Gorsedd Gardens (lawns directly in front of the museum's south-east entrance front). The Portland stone museum facade with its columned portico and steps, framed by the gardens in the foreground. The museum is to the north-west. From here you see the Portland stone facade with its columned portico and steps, framed by the gardens in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the portico in the centre, keeping the building's vertical lines straight by holding your phone level. Leave a band of lawn at the bottom for depth. For a different view, climb the granite steps and frame the entrance between the pillars, or step back into Cathays Park to show the museum with its neighbouring Edwardian buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the pale stone looks washed out against the sky. Take a few shots in case people walk across the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright but not harsh moment so the stone shows its detail. The facade faces south-east, so it is likely to be best lit in the morning. Visit early on a weekday if you want fewer people on the lawns.

text.access_note: The gardens are open public space, but the museum itself is a public building that announced a temporary closure in February 2025, so check the official site for opening times before you go.

name: Cardiff Market
label: Cardiff Market
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27027419: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cardiff Central Market' (108 m across).
notes: Victorian covered market with a glass roof and a gallery.

text.description: Cardiff Market is a Victorian indoor market in the Castle Quarter of the city centre. It is one of the easier places in Cardiff to photograph on a phone, because everything is close and under cover. It opened in May 1891 and was designed by the Borough Surveyor, William Harpur. Inside, a balcony level runs around the walls above the ground-floor stalls, which gives you two heights to shoot from and plenty of old ironwork and roof structure to include. The building has been listed since 1975 and is now Grade II*. Around 60 independent traders work here, selling things like fresh fish, fruit and veg, clothing, music and hardware, so there is always colour and activity. Ashton's the fishmongers, at the Trinity Street entrance, say they have traded here since 1866, and The Market Deli has kept the same stall since 1928. Above the High Street entrance hangs a large H. Samuel clock. The current one dates from 1963, and a clock has hung there since 1910. Look for it on your way in or out. Start with a wide shot of the hall, then move closer to stalls and signs. Ask a stallholder before you photograph them close up. Restoration work was planned from 2024 while the market stays open, so some areas may look different from older pictures.
text.geographic_location: In the Castle Quarter of Cardiff city centre. The entrances are on St Mary Street and Trinity Street, with another from an alleyway off Church Street, and The Hayes is directly outside.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Start from the Castle Quarter in the city centre and head for the St Mary Street or Trinity Street entrance. Once you are in the city centre, follow the signs and the map to the market building. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the market. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole hall and the balcony. Switch to the default lens (1x) for stalls and signs. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the clock and distant details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk the ground floor, then go up to the balcony level for a view down onto the stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the hall straight. Hold the phone level, or the walls will lean inwards. Use the balcony railing or roof ironwork to frame a shot of the stalls below. For the clock, stand back outside the High Street entrance and use 2x or more.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the roof windows don't blow out. If a stall is dimly lit, hold the phone steady against a pillar or rail, or try night mode. Keep portrait mode for stallholders who are happy to be photographed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit during normal trading hours, when the stalls are open and busy. Check the official site for times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a working indoor market, so opening times and works may change; check the official site before you go.

name: Bute Park
label: Bute Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Millennium Bridge' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Millennium Bridge' (way/173632648): middle (63 m across); moved 15 m off water.
notes: Large park along the River Taff behind the castle.

text.description: Bute Park is a big, green stretch of central Cardiff: 130 acres (53 ha) of parkland, tree-lined avenues and gardens that once formed the grounds of Cardiff Castle. It runs along the east bank of the River Taff, which gives you water, trees and open lawns in one frame. The park was laid out from 1873 by Andrew Pettigrew, head gardener to the 3rd Marquess of Bute, and was handed to Cardiff's council in 1947. The park and the castle grounds are listed Grade I for their special historic interest. For a first photo, stand on the Millennium Bridge. From there the red footbridge, the river and the park's trees come together in one easy picture. If you have time, two other places are worth a look. Cooper's Field gives a view of the castle's clock tower rising above mature trees. Blackweir Bridge looks onto the river and a tumbling weir. Along the way you may spot William Burges's Animal Wall, a stone wall topped with sculpted animal heads, and the Summerhouse kiosk, built in 2010. Keep your phone steady and take a few frames of each scene, because the light under the trees changes quickly. Check the official site before you go in case of closures or event set-ups.
text.geographic_location: Bute Park lies in central Cardiff, along the east bank of the River Taff and next to Cardiff Castle. Sophia Gardens and Pontcanna Fields are on the opposite bank, reached by footbridges.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Cardiff city centre and head on foot towards the Summerhouse kiosk by the river. The Millennium Bridge is close to the kiosk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge, river and trees. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in more of the park. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the castle clock tower from Cooper's Field or for details at the weir.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Millennium Bridge (near the Summerhouse kiosk). The red footbridge over the River Taff, framed by the riverside and the park's trees. From here you can photograph the red footbridge over the River Taff, framed by the riverside and the park's trees. The park itself stretches away to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the red bridge along one of the lower lines, with trees on either side. Keep the horizon level. For a different picture, try Cooper's Field, where the castle's clock tower rises above the trees with the acer and camellia collection in front. Blackweir Bridge is another option, with the weir beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out. Try a Live Photo by the weir to catch the moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder on the water and the red of the bridge. Autumn is good for tree colour, but any dry day works.

text.access_note: Bute Park is an open public park, free to enter, but check the official site before you go for any closures or event set-ups.

name: Castle Arcade
label: Castle Arcade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Castle Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Castle Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/95037878: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castle Arcade' (105 m across).
notes: Victorian shopping arcade with independent shops.

text.description:
Castle Arcade is a covered Victorian shopping arcade in the middle of Cardiff. It was begun in 1887 and designed by Edwin Seward for the Bute Estate, as part of the Marquess of Bute's building programme that helped turn Cardiff into a busy commercial centre. It was damaged in the Cardiff Blitz in 1941, but it was restored and still looks Victorian. In 1975 it was listed Grade II*, described as the finest of Cardiff's Victorian arcades.

It photographs well because it is made up of repeating details: shopfronts, signs and a split-level gallery, all drawing the eye down a narrow passage. It runs south from opposite Cardiff Castle, then turns east to come out on High Street. The easiest start is from the Castle Street end, where you can frame the entrance with the castle-side street behind you. This is a quieter, secondary view rather than a postcard shot. For a stronger picture, walk in and go up to the balcony. From there you can look down the length of the shopfronts and the arcade floor below.

Keep your phone steady and let the passage lines lead into the picture. Shop windows and passers-by will change from minute to minute, so take a few frames and pick the best. Because it is indoors, the light depends on the arcade's own lighting.
text.geographic_location: Castle Arcade is in Cardiff city centre, in the Castle Quarter. It starts opposite Cardiff Castle on Castle Street and comes out on High Street.
text.directions_text: Start from Cardiff Castle: the arcade's Castle Street entrance is on the opposite side of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The arcade is a public shopping passage, but opening times and any restrictions are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the entrance, as it looks natural and keeps the shopfronts in proportion. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arcade's ceiling and sides in a narrow space, but keep the phone level so the lines do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Castle Street (the arcade's end opposite Cardiff Castle). The arcade's entrance opening from the castle end, framing the Victorian arcade interior against the castle-side street. From here you see the entrance opening out, with the Victorian interior framed against the castle-side street. For a better view, go inside and up to the arcade balcony, which looks down the split-level gallery and the shopfronts below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arcade entrance in the centre, so the sides and roof lines lead the eye inwards. If you go up to the balcony, shoot along the length of the arcade and keep the shopfronts parallel to the edges of the frame. Take a vertical shot to include the roof and floor together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the arcade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so bright windows or lights do not wash out. If the light is dim, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or rail to keep it still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a quieter time of day, when there are fewer people in the passage, and go while the shops are open so the arcade looks lively. Check opening times before you go.

name: Mermaid Quay
label: Mermaid Quay
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Roald Dahl Plass' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Roald Dahl Plass' (relation/11005399): middle (123 m across).

notes: Waterfront promenade with cafes and views of the bay.

text.description:
Mermaid Quay is the waterfront shopping and leisure area on the edge of Cardiff Bay, with restaurants, bars, cafes and shops in a development of about 14,000 square metres. It was designed by Benoy and opened in August 1999, the same year the Cardiff Bay Barrage was completed. Before the barrage, the bay was tidal, with wide mud flats at low tide. It is now a freshwater lake of around 500 acres, and that still water is part of why the area photographs well.

The best view is from Roald Dahl Plass, the open oval plaza next to the quay. From there the Mermaid Quay buildings run along one side of the plaza, with the Wales Millennium Centre beyond and the bay's waterfront buildings around the edges. The curved shape of the plaza gives you a natural frame, and the buildings stay sharp and clear even on a phone. The plaza has also appeared in Doctor Who and Torchwood, so you may spot fans taking pictures too.

For a second view, the Cardiff Bay Barrage shows the quay from across the water at a distance, with the bay and the St David's Hotel in the same shot. Check the map for the exact viewing spot. Keep the plaza wide and uncluttered in your photo, and wait a moment for passers-by to clear the middle if you want an empty foreground.
text.geographic_location: Mermaid Quay is in the Cardiff Bay area of Cardiff, on the waterfront beside Roald Dahl Plass, with the Wales Millennium Centre just beyond. The quay's own car park is opposite Techniquest.
text.directions_text: From Cardiff city centre, head south to Cardiff Bay by train to Cardiff Bay station, by Cardiff Bus (including the BayCar), by waterbus, or on the off-road cycle route. Mermaid Quay is to the south-west of it, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

name: Roald Dahl Plass
label: Roald Dahl Plass
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Roald Dahl Plass' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Roald Dahl Plass' (relation/11005399): middle (123 m across).

notes: Open waterfront plaza with the Water Tower sculpture.

text.description:
Roald Dahl Plass is a big oval open space in Cardiff Bay, and it works well for phone photos because everything around it is built to be looked at. A ring of illuminated pillars frames the plaza, the Wales Millennium Centre's bronze dome closes the view at one end, and the Pierhead Building sits to one side. The Water Tower, a metal fountain about 21 m high, stands at the northern end. Its water runs down in an intermittent stream, so it is worth waiting for a moment when it is flowing.

The oval is the old dock. West Bute Dock opened in 1839 and was one of the places that made Cardiff a huge coal port. The last coal left the dock in 1964, and it was later filled in. The artist William Pye and Nicholas Hare Architects designed the space as the Oval Basin, which opened in April 2000. It was renamed after the Cardiff-born author Roald Dahl in 2002. Fans of Doctor Who and Torchwood may also know the tower from the programmes.

The classic shot looks south-west from near the northern end, with the dome filling the background and the Pierhead on the right. For a second picture, turn round and frame the Water Tower with the pillars beside it. The Plass is used for events, so stalls or crowds can block the view at times.
text.geographic_location: In Cardiff Bay, on the coast to the south of Cardiff city centre, with the Wales Millennium Centre and the Senedd nearby.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head south from the city centre to Cardiff Bay and look for Roald Dahl Plass. The Water Tower is just to the north, about 1 minute on foot from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the postcard view of the plaza, dome and Pierhead. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the pillars and the whole curve of the oval. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dome or the Water Tower on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass (near the Plass's northern end, looking south-west toward the Wales Millennium Centre). The oval plaza running up to the Wales Millennium Centre's bronze dome, with the Pierhead Building to one side. From there you see the oval plaza running up to the Wales Millennium Centre's bronze dome, with the Pierhead Building to one side. The Water Tower is just behind you to the north, so turn round for a second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower line so the dome and sky get most of the picture. Keep the Pierhead on the right edge, as in the usual postcard view. For an alternative, turn north and frame the Water Tower with the cascade and the illuminated pillars beside it. Another option is the view from the waterside end, looking up the lowered walkway towards the pillars and the Millennium Centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome or tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bronze and the sky do not wash out. For the Water Tower, a Live Photo can catch the water moving. If you shoot after dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the Plass is quiet so people do not fill the foreground. The pillars are illuminated, so it is worth checking how they look at different times.

text.access_note: This is an open public square, but events can fence off or fill parts of it, so check the official site before you go if you are planning around a particular view.

text.description:
The Norwegian Church Arts Centre is a white timber church on the edge of Cardiff Bay, and it is one of the easiest buildings on the waterfront to photograph. The pale wooden walls stand out well against the open water behind them, and the Mermaid Quay area gives a busy, colourful background without crowding the church itself. Photo guides single out the white wooden exterior with the bay as a backdrop as the best shot here, and the outside of the church is described as a good place to take in wide views over the bay.

The best-known picture is taken from the outdoor terrace on the bay side of the building. From there the church is in front of you and the water opens out behind it. If you want something with more history in the background, Pier Head is also suggested as a possible viewpoint, with the Pierhead Building behind the church, though the exact spot is not pinned down, so check the map. That would be a more traditional backdrop than the modern bay.

For a phone, this is an easy stop. Take one wide shot to show the whole scene, then step in for a closer one of the timber walls and windows. Check for people on the terrace before you shoot, as the church has its own café and events, and they may affect how much of the terrace you can use. Opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
The Pierhead Building is a Grade I listed landmark on the edge of Cardiff Bay. It was built in 1897 for the Bute Dock Company and designed by William Frame, who had trained under William Burges. The red glazed terracotta, the carved friezes, the gargoyles, the hexagonal chimneys and the tall clock tower give it a busy, decorative outline that suits a phone camera. The clock is nicknamed "Baby Big Ben". A coat of arms on the front carries the old company motto, "Wrth ddŵr a thân" (by water and fire), a nod to the steam power behind the docks. Today the building belongs to the Senedd estate and works as a museum and event space.

From there you see the south-facing frontage and clock tower across the water, and the Ivor Novello statue can sit in the foreground to add scale. The building is tall and fairly close, so shoot it upright rather than sideways. If you have time, there is a second, more distant view from Pierhead Street, where the whole building can be pulled in with the zoom. Take a few frames from each place, as the two views feel quite different.
text.geographic_location: The Pierhead Building stands in Cardiff Bay, beside the Senedd building and facing the water. The viewing spot on Roald Dahl Plass is at the entrance to the West Bute Dock, east of the Industrial and Maritime Museum.
text.directions_text: Head for Cardiff Bay and look for Roald Dahl Plass, the square at the entrance to the West Bute Dock, east of the Industrial and Maritime Museum. If you want the distant view, walk back to Pierhead Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) from where you stand so the whole frontage and clock tower fit. Use the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched look. From Pierhead Street, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass (Square at the entrance to the West Bute Dock, east of the Industrial and Maritime Museum). The south-facing red-brick frontage and clock tower of the Pierhead across the bay, with the Ivor Novello statue in the foreground. The Pierhead's red-brick south-facing frontage and clock tower are across the bay, with the Ivor Novello statue close by to use in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright (portrait orientation) so the tower and the front fit in one frame. Put the statue low in the foreground to add depth, and switch on gridlines to keep the tower straight. For a more distant view, walk to Pierhead Street and use the telephoto lens to bring the building in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the brick to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the clock tower and the bright sky keep their detail. Keep the phone level to avoid leaning verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Summer evenings are a good choice if you want the Cardiff Bay Ferris wheel lit up in the frame, which works best from the side of the building. Otherwise pick a day with clear light on the front.

text.description: The Royal Arcade is the oldest shopping arcade in Cardiff. It was built in 1858 and is Grade II listed. It runs east to west between The Hayes and St Mary Street, and part of it passes under the old David Morgan's department store. The best first picture is from outside, on The Hayes. From there you can see the three-storey Pennant stone and red brick entrance front, with its central canopy and the shopfronts at street level. The facade is distinctive, so it makes a tidy, well-balanced frame on a phone. Step inside and the view changes: the glass-and-metal roof, the shopfronts on both sides and the ornate ceiling detail all lead the eye down the passage. The arcade was refurbished in 2007-2008, and a few first-floor Venetian windows and original wooden storefronts survive. There are still independent shops here, including Wally's Delicatessen and sellers of Welsh textiles, gifts and homeware. These add colour to a photo and give you something to point the phone at. Photography inside is generally fine, but ask shop staff before you spend long shooting. At busy times, keep the phone handheld and move quickly so you don't block the narrow passage. Take one frame of the entrance front from The Hayes, then walk in for a second, looking-down-the-arcade shot.
text.geographic_location: In Cardiff city centre, running between The Hayes and St Mary Street, close to Cardiff Central Library and opposite the St David's 2 development.
text.directions_text: Head for The Hayes in the middle of Cardiff, opposite the St David's 2 development and close to Cardiff Central Library. The entrance is directly opposite where you stand. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

If the pavement is crowded and you can't step back, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade in. Inside the arcade, the ultra-wide (0.5x) is good for the roof and the long view of shopfronts. The telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) is useful for ornate details above the shopfronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on The Hayes (opposite the arcade's Grade II entrance block, at the south end of Morgan's department store). The three-storey Pennant stone and red brick entrance front of the arcade, with its central canopy and shopfronts at street level. The arcade lies to the west of you. shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and the stonework keep their detail. Inside, tap on the shopfronts and nudge the slider up a little if the arcade looks dim.

text.description: Cardiff City Hall is part of the Cathays Park civic centre, a white Portland stone building in the Edwardian Baroque style. It opened on 29 October 1906 and is Grade I listed. It photographs well because the gardens give you a layered scene: flower beds, a fountain and trees in front, then the stone walls, the dome and the clock tower rising behind. The tower is 59 m high, and each of its four faces has a gilded dial 3.7 m across, so it stands out clearly against the sky. The best-known view is head-on across the fountain pool, whose fountains date from 1969. For a gentler, more garden-like picture, walk into Alexandra Gardens, where the back of the building faces the park. Spring is especially pretty when the cherry blossom is out, and the central fountain and its reflections give you something to frame the building with. Keep your phone level so the tall walls and tower don't lean, and take a few shots from different spots around the water. If you want the full line-up of civic buildings, a wider view across Cathays Park shows City Hall as one of a row. Early morning is usually quieter, with fewer people crossing your picture.
text.geographic_location: City Hall stands in the Cathays Park civic centre in central Cardiff. Alexandra Gardens is the park behind the building.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit flower beds, fountain and building in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock tower and its gilded dials.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Alexandra Gardens (inside the gardens behind the building, where the rear of City Hall faces the park). The civic building rising behind flower beds, fountain and trees, with the clock tower in view. Behind the building, where the rear of City Hall faces the park. From here the building rises behind flower beds, fountain and trees, with the clock tower in view. For the head-on view across the fountain pool at the front, walk round to the entrance side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put flowers or blossom low in the frame, then let the fountain and trees lead the eye up to the dome and clock tower. Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't tilt. If the water is calm, include some reflection. As an alternative, step back into Cathays Park to show City Hall as part of the row of civic buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone and sky keep their detail. Try portrait mode on a close flower bed, but switch it off for the building itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring, for the cherry blossom, and early morning for fewer people in the frame.

text.description:
The Welsh National War Memorial stands in Alexandra Gardens, in Cathays Park, and it is one of the most dignified places in Cardiff to point a phone. It is a circular colonnade of pale stone around a sunken court. At the centre, three bronze figures (a soldier, a sailor and an airman) stand around a stone pylon, each holding a wreath aloft. A winged figure of Victory crowns the top. Sir Ninian Comper designed it and the Prince of Wales unveiled it on 12 June 1928. It remembers those who died in the First World War, and a plaque for the Second World War was added in 1949. It is Grade II* listed.

The round colonnade and the formal gardens make tidy, balanced pictures. The classic straight-on view down the central path of Alexandra Gardens is the best place to start. For something a little different, you could try a layered view using the Memorial to Welsh Volunteers in the Spanish Civil War. Check on site for its exact position in the gardens. If you find it, stand by it and look back toward the colonnade, so the smaller stone memorial fills the foreground and the big colonnade sits behind. Keep the horizon level using your gridlines, and leave a little space around the colonnade so the columns are not cut off. This is a place of remembrance, so be thoughtful: avoid intrusive shots during commemorative events.
text.geographic_location: In Alexandra Gardens, part of Cathays Park, Cardiff.
text.directions_text: Head to Alexandra Gardens in Cathays Park, Cardiff. Walk into the gardens and follow the central path to the circular colonnade. The Memorial to Welsh Volunteers in the Spanish Civil War is also in the gardens, so check on site for its exact position. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the central-axis view at the phone icon on the map. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole colonnade and gardens, and keep it level. Telephoto (2x or more) is good for the bronze figures. If you try the optional layered view with the Spanish Civil War memorial in front, 1x is also a good starting point, but check the view on site.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. As an optional extra, walk to the Memorial to Welsh Volunteers in the Spanish Civil War in the gardens (check its exact position on site) and look back toward the colonnade. This view is not pinned on the map.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: For the classic shot, use the central path of Alexandra Gardens, which leads the eye to the colonnade. Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines. If you try the optional layered view, put the Spanish Civil War memorial low in the frame and let the colonnade sit behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the colonnade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale stone keeps its detail against the sky. If you try the layered view and want the foreground sharp as well, tap on the foreground memorial instead and check how the background looks.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in the gardens. Avoid commemorative events if you want a quiet, unobtrusive shot.

name: Animal Wall
label: Animal Wall

text.description:
The Animal Wall is a row of carved stone animals that seem to be clambering along the top of a wall beside Castle Street, with Bute Park behind them. It was designed by the architect William Burges in the 1860s for the third Marquess of Bute, but it was not built until around 1890, after Burges had died. The sculptor Thomas Nicholls carved the first animals, including lions, a bear, baboons and a seal. Alexander Carrick added six more in 1931, among them a pelican, an anteater and a beaver. The wall was moved about 50 metres to its present spot when the road in front of the castle was widened. It is Grade I listed, and the animals were restored in 2010, when the anteater's nose and the missing glass eyes were replaced.

It photographs well because each animal has its own character and the wall gives you a repeating pattern to work with. The pavement runs alongside it, so you can walk the length and pick your favourites. Stand on the pavement to the left of the main castle entrance, facing the castle, for a close, straight-on view of the animals appearing to climb over the wall from the park side. This is the best spot for detail shots. For a wider picture of the whole row with the park's greenery behind, walk a little way along Castle Street. Keep an eye on passing people and traffic, and take your time to get a clean frame.
text.geographic_location: In the Castle Quarter of Cardiff city centre, on Castle Street beside Cardiff Castle, along the edge of Bute Park.
text.directions_text: Head for Cardiff Castle in the city centre; the wall is just to the west of the main castle entrance, on Castle Street along the edge of Bute Park. The phone icon on the map is on the pavement to the left of the main castle entrance, facing the castle. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for close, straight-on shots of the animals. Switch to 2x or more to pick out a single face without stepping into the pavement. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole row, and keep the phone level so the wall does not bend.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the animals look as if they are climbing over the wall from the park side, and the pavement runs parallel to the wall so they are easy to see.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Fill the frame with one or two animals and keep the phone square-on to the wall for a clean, close image. Turn on gridlines to line up the top of the wall. For a different view, walk along Castle Street and shoot the whole row of stone animals with the park's greenery behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on an animal's face to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the pale stone looks too bright. Portrait mode can work on a single animal, but check that the edges of the stone stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight shows off the carving best. Early in the day the pavement is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The wall stands on a public pavement along Castle Street, so it is free to view from outside; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit the castle or park.

label: St John's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Church Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Church Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/90484757: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. John The Baptist Church' (63 m across).
notes: Medieval church with a tall tower in the city centre.

text.description:
St John the Baptist Church is a Grade I listed parish church in the middle of Cardiff. Apart from Cardiff Castle, it is the only medieval building left in the city centre, so it stands out among the shops and newer buildings around it. The church dates back to 1180. It was rebuilt in the later 1400s after being sacked in 1404, and the tall pinnacled tower is usually dated to about 1490. The tower is over 40 metres high and has a crown of openwork battlements, which makes a strong shape against the sky.

The classic view is from Church Street, where the tower closes the end of the street. The street frames it neatly, and the rest of the scene is simple city-centre buildings, so the tower is clearly the subject. Trinity Street gives a more side-on view of the tower and the west end of the church. The churchyard garden shows the church from behind, with old gravestones in the foreground.

On a phone, the tower's height is the main challenge. Take a wide view first to get the whole street and tower in, then step in or zoom for the stonework, battlements and pinnacles. Keep people and passing traffic in mind: a few figures in the street can help show the scale, but a busy moment can clutter the frame.
text.geographic_location: In the city centre of Cardiff, at the end of Church Street, close to Trinity Street and Working Street. The church sits next to the path that links Working Street with Cardiff Central Market.
text.directions_text: Make your way on foot to the centre of Cardiff and head for Church Street. Once you have the classic view, Trinity Street is just alongside the church if you want a second angle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the street and tower together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole tower will not fit, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the battlements and pinnacles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Church Street (looking down the street toward the church tower). The church tower closing the end of the street, the classic straight-on view from the city-centre approach. From here the church tower closes the end of the street, which is the straight-on postcard view coming in from the city centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with the centre of the frame so the tower sits in the middle and the verticals stay straight. Keep the phone level, because tilting it up makes the tower lean. For a different angle, Trinity Street shows the tower and the west end of the church from the side, and the churchyard garden gives a rear view with old gravestones in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the grey stone keeps its detail. Use the telephoto lens rather than pinching to digital zoom for the pinnacles, as it keeps the image sharper.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, when the street is likely to be quieter, is a good time for a clear straight-on view. Soft daylight suits the grey stone best.

text.access_note: Church Street is an ordinary public street; the church interior and churchyard garden may have set opening times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Church Street is a public street where you can stand and photograph freely.
The street is likely to be quieter early in the day.
Soft daylight suits the grey stone of the tower.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean.
The church interior and churchyard garden may only be open at certain times.
